title: Friday, 4:45 p.m.
note: Fictional patients. Your program’s written urgent-call protocol is the authority; only clinicians give medicine instructions.
intro: You are the transplant coordinator. At 4:45 p.m. on Friday, Ms. Joy Navarro, 29, three months after transplant, texts the clinic number: “The pharmacy has no tacrolimus until Monday. I’ll just restart on Monday, ok?”

choices.text: “Please do not stop or stretch your doses. A doctor from the team will call you within the hour.” Log it with two identifiers and a callback number, and route it to the on-call transplant clinician now.
choices.feedback: A missed immunosuppressant is a same-day route under the protocol. Running out for even a few days can trigger rejection. Never tell a caller to take, skip, delay, or double a medicine outside the protocol.

choices.text: “OK, three days should be fine. Restart Monday.”
choices.feedback: That is medicine advice, outside your role, and it is wrong: three days without tacrolimus three months after transplant risks rejection.
choices.then: You text again: “Please wait, a doctor will call you.” Then you route it.

choices.feedback: She may find one, but a supply gap is an emergency in slow motion. The team needs to arrange an authorized continuity plan today.
choices.then: You route it to the on-call clinician as well.

n2.scene: The laboratory calls: Mr. Leo Bautista, five months after transplant, has a creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL today. His last result was 1.2. The report will also be emailed.

choices.text: Treat it as an urgent call: log it and route it to the on-call transplant clinician now.
choices.feedback: A doubled creatinine can be the first sign of rejection, which usually causes no symptoms. An abnormal result triggers a call, not a filing.

choices.text: File the emailed report for the clinic on Monday.
choices.feedback: Rejection found late has fewer options. A result like this is routed the same day.

choices.text: Call Mr. Bautista and ask how he feels before deciding.
choices.feedback: His symptoms help, but rejection is often silent. The clinician decides what the number means; route it first.
choices.then: He feels well. You route the result at 17:15.

vitals.oncall: Dr. Ramos: no reply in 15 min

n3.scene: You paged Dr. Ramos and posted both calls in the transplant group chat at 17:05. Fifteen minutes later, no reply. The protocol’s response time is 15 minutes.

choices.text: Escalate to the backup on the list, Dr. Lim, by phone; a group chat post is dispatch, not closure.
choices.feedback: If the clinician does not respond within the protocol’s time, escalate to the backup. A text, voicemail, or chat message only sends the problem; it does not close it.
choices.then: Dr. Lim answers at 17:22. Ms. Navarro is to collect a supply from the center’s pharmacy tonight; Mr. Bautista is to come to the emergency department for assessment.

choices.text: Wait; the chat shows the message was seen.
choices.feedback: “Seen” is not “acted.” Two patients are waiting on a decision.
choices.then: At 17:40 you call Dr. Lim, who gives both plans.

choices.feedback: One more try is reasonable, but the protocol time has passed. Escalate to the backup.
choices.then: No answer again. You call Dr. Lim, who gives both plans.

vitals.call3: Donor’s wife: wound red, oozing, fever

n4.scene: Mrs. Liza Bautista calls about her husband, Mr. Leo Bautista’s brother and his kidney donor, two weeks after nephrectomy. His wound is red and oozing and he has a fever. “And please tell Leo’s doctor too, so they know.”

choices.text: Open a separate urgent-call log in the donor’s record and route it to the donor surgical team; explain kindly that his information goes only to his own team.
choices.feedback: The donor has his own team. Two people, two logs, two routes, even from one family. The donor’s information stays in the donor’s record.

choices.text: Add it to Mr. Bautista’s call so one doctor sees both.
choices.feedback: That routes the donor through the recipient’s team and puts his information in another person’s record.
choices.then: You separate it and route it to the donor surgical team.

choices.text: Tell her to take him to any emergency department.
choices.feedback: Urgent care may be right, but the donor surgical team must know and decide. Log and route it.
choices.then: You log it and route it to the donor surgical team, who give the plan.

choices.text: When the clinician has received it, given a plan, the patient has repeated the plan back, and the log shows times and who decided; then check later that each patient arrived or collected the medicine.
choices.feedback: Received, acted, understood, documented. Anything less is an open urgent call. Checking that the plan happened closes it for real.

choices.text: When the message has been sent to the clinician.
choices.feedback: Sending is dispatch. A call is closed when the patient has the plan and you have documented it.

choices.text: When the clinician has given a plan.
choices.feedback: Close, but the patient must also understand the plan (repeat it back), and the log must show it.

end.title: 8:30 p.m.
end.text: Ms. Navarro collected her tacrolimus at 7:10 p.m. Mr. Leo Bautista was admitted for assessment of his kidney. His brother was seen by the donor surgical team and started on treatment for a wound infection. Each log shows the times, who decided, the plan, and your follow-up check.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Route by protocol. Missed immunosuppressants and a rising creatinine are same-day calls.
  • Never give medicine advice outside protocol.
  • A chat message is dispatch, not closure. Escalate to the backup when the response time passes.
  • Donors have their own team. Two people, two logs, two routes.
  • Close the loop: received, acted, understood, documented, and checked.

See Protocol, not advice, The donor has their own team and From call to confirmed plan.
